did_you_know.text: Did you know? Isaiah describes Damascus as a city that will lose its status and become a ruin—a prophecy portraying the destruction of Aram’s political center.
Did you know? The cities of Aroer are described as so deserted that they become places where flocks lie down, with no one to disturb them.
Did you know? The prophecy mentions Damascus and Ephraim together: Ephraim’s fortress will disappear, the kingdom of Damascus will cease to exist, and the remnant of Aram will lose its status.
Did you know? Jacob’s condition is described through a bodily image: his glory will fade and his strength will waste away, meaning that his power and prosperity will decline.
Did you know? Isaiah compares Jacob’s poverty to a field after the harvest, where only a few ears of grain remain, and he also mentions the Valley of Rephaim.
Did you know? Even after an olive tree is beaten, only two or three olives remain at the top of a branch, with a few more on its fruit-bearing branches—a picture of a tiny remnant.
Did you know? In the midst of the crisis, a turning point appears: people will look to their Maker, and their eyes will turn to the Holy One of Israel.
Did you know? Turning to the Lord is also described as abandoning human-made altars and objects of worship made with their fingers, including the Asherahs and incense altars.

Did you know? The prophet connects forgetting the God of salvation with the failure of their plantings: the plants and seeds may sprout quickly, but in the end they will produce a meager harvest and bring sorrow.

Did you know? The enemy nations are compared to the roaring of the sea and the raging of mighty waters, but in the following verses the Lord rebukes them and scatters them like chaff; their downfall comes before morning.
